sentences.text: Giganotosaurus is considered one of the largest theropod dinosaurs known to science.
The holotype has been estimated at 12 to 13 meters long and over 4 meters high at the hips, while weight estimates for the same skeleton range from 4.2 to 13.8 tons.
Its teeth were compressed sideways and featured serrations, and the premaxilla possessed four tooth sockets, a feature shared with Acrocanthosaurus and Sinraptor.
The shoulder girdle of Giganotosaurus was proportionally shorter than that of Tyrannosaurus.

Estimates of its skull length differ: the holotype skull was first put at 1.8 meters and later corrected to 1.56 meters, a larger dentary bone suggests a skull up to 1.95 meters long, and extrapolations from a related species give 1.634 meters, one of the largest theropod skulls known.
A 2007 study concluded that the largest theropods, Giganotosaurus among them, had reached the maximum possible size for a strictly bipedal animal.

Coria suggested that a bonebed of Mapusaurus, a close relative of Giganotosaurus, was the result of a catastrophic event, and that its mostly medium-sized individuals, with very few young or old, suggested that these large theropods may have lived and hunted in groups.
The genus Giganotosaurus was described by Coria and Salgado in 1995.
The holotype specimen was discovered in the Candeleros Formation of Patagonia in 1993 by the fossil hunter Rubén Darío Carolini while driving a dune buggy near Villa El Chocón in Argentina.
Giganotosaurus is thought to have been homeothermic with a metabolism between that of a mammal and a reptile, enabling fast growth.
The jaw joint sat far behind the neck attachment point compared to other theropods, and the curvature of the lower jaw indicates that Giganotosaurus had a wide mouth.
It had a strong neck with a robust axis vertebra, and the rear neck vertebrae had short, flattened bodies with almost hemispherical front articulations.
While absolute bite force values in newtons were impossible to estimate, Giganotosaurus had a weaker bite force than Tyrannosaurus.
In 1999 and 2002, paleontologist Reese E. Barrick and geologist William J. Showers found that Giganotosaurus had oxygen isotope patterns similar to Tyrannosaurus.

Fossil tracks that may belong to Giganotosaurus range from 36 cm to 50 cm in length with paces between 100 cm and 130 cm, and the footprints are three-toed with large, coarse digits and prominent impressions of claws.
The hind legs had a femur longer than the tibia, indicating strong support but not high speed.
Giganotosaurus was likely the apex predator of its ecosystem.
Coria and Salgado originally classified Giganotosaurus as belonging to the Tetanurae clade rather than basal theropods like ceratosaurs.
Giganotosaurus belongs to the family Carcharodontosauridae, as found, for example, by a 2016 study by Apesteguía et al.
The Candeleros Formation containing Giganotosaurus fossils was composed of sandstones deposited in fluvial and aeolian environments.

It is debated whether Giganotosaurus was larger than Tyrannosaurus, roughly equal in size, or if its largest size estimates are exaggerated. In 1997, Coria estimated Giganotosaurus to be 13.7 to 14.3 meters long and weigh 8 to 10 metric tons, larger than Carcharodontosaurus, while a large dentary bone suggests that some individuals may have reached a weight of 10 metric tons, making them potentially larger than Tyrannosaurus.
